heading.v: What is an Identity Protection (IP) PIN?

t.v: The

is a 6-digit number assigned to eligible individuals to help prevent the misuse of their Social Security number or Individual Taxpayer Identification Number on fraudulent federal income tax returns. A new IP PIN will be generated each year.

If the IRS assigned you (or anyone on your tax return) an IP PIN, you must use it to confirm your identity on any return filed during the current calendar year. This includes current year returns as well as any delinquent tax returns.

heading.v: How is blindness defined?

t.v: For tax purposes, you are considered blind if one of these applies:
You don’t have any eyesight.
You can’t see better than 20/200 in your better eye with glasses or contact lenses.
Your field of vision is 20 degrees or less.

If you aren’t totally blind, you must get a certified statement from an eye doctor stating that one of these is true:
You can’t see better than 20/200 in the better eye with glasses or contact lenses.
Your field of vision is 20 degrees or less.

heading.v: What’s considered full time?

t.v: A full-time student is someone who meets their school’s full-time attendance requirements for 5 months in a calendar year. The 5 months don’t have to be consecutive. Also, the 5 months don’t have to be 5 full months. For example, a student starting a semester mid-January and graduating mid-May attends the school for 5 months.
The student must go to a school with:
A regular teaching staff
A course of study
An enrolled student body
A school includes:
High schools
Colleges
Universities
Technical, trade, and mechanical schools
Full-time, on-farm training courses offered through a school or a state, county, or local government agency
A school doesn’t include:
On-the-job training courses
Correspondence schools
Organizations offering only internet courses

heading.v: How does the IRS define being married?

t.v: Many long-term partnerships are like marriage. For tax purposes, here’s what is and isn’t considered married.
You’re considered married if you’re:
Married and living together
Living together in a common law marriage that’s recognized in your state or in the state where you entered into the common law marriage
Married and living apart but not legally separated under a decree of divorce or separate maintenance
Separated under an interlocutory (not final) decree of divorce
You’re not considered married if you:
Are in a registered domestic partnership
Are in a civil union
Obtained a final decree of divorce or separate maintenance by December 31,
Have a court decree of annulment (this also applies to past tax years as the marriage never existed)

heading.v: What should I consider when deciding to file jointly or file separately?

t.v: Here are a few things that can help you decide if it’s better to file jointly (using Married Filing Jointly filing status) or file separately (using Married Filing Separately filing status).
If you and your spouse decide to file jointly, your tax may be lower than your combined tax if you file separately. This means you’ll probably get more money back or owe less.
This is because the
and tax brackets change when two people combine their income and expenses on a joint return. You can file a joint return even if one of you had no income or deductions.

However, filing separately can sometimes mean you pay less tax. For example, if you have high medical expenses, you may be able to deduct more of those expenses. This is because when you file separately, you’re reporting less income, which may qualify you to deduct more.

If you file a separate return, some credits and deductions aren’t available or can be reduced. For example, taxpayers filing separate returns are generally not eligible for the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) unless they have a qualifying child and are separated from their spouse. Taxpayers filing separate returns will also pay tax on more of their social security benefits.

If you and your spouse decide to file a joint return and one spouse doesn’t pay the tax due, the other may have to. Or, if one spouse doesn’t report the correct tax, both spouses may be responsible for any additional taxes assessed by the IRS. One spouse may be held responsible for all the tax due even if all the income was earned by the other spouse.
You may want to file separately if:
You believe your spouse isn’t reporting all of their income
You don’t want to be responsible for any taxes due if your spouse doesn’t have enough tax withheld or doesn’t pay enough estimated tax

If you and your spouse decide to file a joint return, all or part of your portion of the refund can be applied (offset) to your spouse’s legally enforceable past-due federal tax, state income tax, state unemployment compensation debts, child support, or a federal nontax debt, such as a student loan. If this happens, you can file
to claim injured spouse relief to get back your share of the joint refund.

heading.v: What’s the difference between the standard deduction and itemizing?

t.v: Deductions reduce how much of your income gets taxed. When you itemize deductions, you individually list each allowed expense and then reduce your taxable income by the total. The standard deduction is an alternative that allows you to reduce your taxable income by a set amount, without listing expenses.

For many taxpayers the standard deduction amount is higher than the amount they’d get by itemizing. But when your individual deductions total more than the amount of the standard deduction, it’s more advantageous to itemize.

heading.v: What’s considered full time?

t.v: A full-time student is someone who meets their school’s full-time attendance requirements for 5 months in a calendar year. The 5 months don’t have to be consecutive. A regular teaching staff
A course of study
An enrolled student body
A school includes:
High schools
Colleges
Universities
Technical, trade, and mechanical schools
Full-time, on-farm training courses offered through a school or a state, county, or local government agency
A school doesn’t include:
On-the-job training courses
Correspondence schools
Organizations offering only internet courses

is your total income minus certain expenses and payments.

Direct File will calculate your AGI after you provide more information about your income and deductions, but for now, you can estimate your AGI by:
Estimating your total income
Subtracting the educator expenses adjustment, if you think you might qualify (maximum $300 per taxpayer)
Subtracting the student loan interest deduction, if you think you might qualify (maximum $2,500 total)

heading.v: Who is the custodial parent?

t.v: The custodial parent is the parent with whom the child lived for the greater number of nights during the year. The other parent is the noncustodial parent.

If the parents divorced or separated during the year and the child lived with both parents before the separation, the custodial parent is the one with whom the child lived for the greater number of nights during the rest of the year.
A child is considered as living with a parent for a night if the child sleeps either:
At that parent’s home, even if the parent isn’t present
In that parent’s presence outside of the parent’s home (for example, when the parent and the child are on vacation together)
If the child lived with each parent for an equal number of nights during the year, the custodial parent is the parent with the higher Adjusted Gross Income (AGI).
If a child is emancipated under state law, the child is treated as not living with either parent.

If a child wasn’t with either parent on a particular night (for example, the child was staying at a friend’s house), the child is treated as living with the parent with whom the child normally would have lived for that night, except for the absence. But if it can’t be determined with which parent the child normally would have lived or if the child would not have lived with either parent that night, the child is treated as not living with either parent that night.

If, due to a parent’s nighttime work schedule, a child lives for a greater number of days, but not nights, with the parent who works at night, that parent is treated as the custodial parent. On a school day, the child is treated as living at the primary residence registered with the school.

c.v: Filing statuses available to married taxpayers

t.v: Generally, married taxpayers can use the Married Filing Jointly or Married Filing Separately filing statuses.

Married taxpayers may also be able to use the Head of Household filing status if they’re considered unmarried for tax purposes and have a qualifying person that meets all of the requirements for that filing status.

t.v: Your filing status helps determine your tax rate. A lower tax rate generally means that less of your income is taxed.

Tax rates are usually the lowest for the Married Filing Jointly filing status. If you qualify for the Head of Household and Married Filing Separately filing status, the tax rate for Married Filing Jointly is still usually the lowest.
Tax rates for the Head of Household filing status are usually lower than tax rates for the Married Filing Separately filing status.

heading.v: What should I consider when deciding to file jointly or file separately?

t.v: Here are a few things that can help you decide if it’s better to file jointly (using Married Filing Jointly filing status) or file separately (using Married Filing Separately filing status).
If you and your spouse decide to file jointly, your tax may be lower than your combined tax if you file separately. This means you’ll probably get more money back or owe less.
This is because the
and tax brackets change when two people combine their income and expenses on a joint return. You can file a joint return even if one of you had no income or deductions.

However, filing separately can sometimes mean you pay less tax. For example, if you have high medical expenses, you may be able to deduct more of those expenses. This is because when you file separately, you’re reporting less income, which may qualify you to deduct more.

If you file a separate return, some credits and deductions aren’t available or can be reduced. For example, taxpayers filing separate returns are generally not eligible for the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) unless they have a qualifying child and are separated from their spouse. Taxpayers filing separate returns will also pay tax on more of their social security benefits.

If you and your spouse decide to file a joint return and one spouse doesn’t pay the tax due, the other may have to. Or, if one spouse doesn’t report the correct tax, both spouses may be responsible for any additional taxes assessed by the IRS. One spouse may be held responsible for all the tax due even if all the income was earned by the other spouse.
You may want to file separately if:
You believe your spouse isn’t reporting all of their income
You don’t want to be responsible for any taxes due if your spouse doesn’t have enough tax withheld or doesn’t pay enough estimated tax

If you and your spouse decide to file a joint return, all or part of your portion of the refund can be applied (offset) to your spouse’s legally enforceable past-due federal tax, state income tax, state unemployment compensation debts, child support, or a federal nontax debt, such as a student loan. If this happens, you can file
to claim injured spouse relief to get back your share of the joint refund.

heading.v: What counts as a foreign financial account?

t.v: Financial accounts are
Bank accounts such as savings and checking accounts, and time deposits
Securities accounts, such as brokerage accounts, securities derivatives accounts, or other financial instruments accounts
Commodity futures or options accounts
Insurance or annuity policies with a cash value (such as a whole life insurance policy)

c.v: How do I know if an account is considered foreign?

t.v: Where the account itself is physically located determines if it is considered a foreign financial account. The account location, not the nationality of the financial institution, is what counts for this question.
Examples:
A savings account at a U.S. bank that is maintained with a branch physically located in France is an example of a foreign account
A savings account at a French bank that is maintained with a branch physically located in the U.S. is not foreign

heading.v: What is a financial interest or signature authority?

t.v: You have a financial interest in a financial account if
you’re the owner of record or holder of legal title (even if the account is maintained for someone else’s benefit)
the owner of record or holder of legal title is your agent or representative or someone else acting on your behalf with respect to the account
the owner of record or holder of legal title is an entity (including a corporation, partnership, or trust) in which you have certain direct or indirect interest

c.v: Learn more about financial interest in foreign financial accounts.

t.v: You have "signature authority" over a financial account if you (alone or together with someone else) have authority to control the disposition of the assets in the account by direct communication with the financial institution maintaining the account.

heading.v: What counts as a foreign trust?

t.v: A trust is a legal document in which someone dictates how their assets get transferred to others. People who create a trust, also known as "grantors," authorize certain individuals or institutions to hold, manage, and distribute assets they put in trust for beneficiaries, like charities or family members. Assets can include things like money, property, accounts, and more.

c.v: How do I know if a trust is considered foreign?

t.v: Unless
of the following are true of a trust, it’s considered foreign:
a court in the United States exercises primary supervision over the trust; and
one or more United States persons have authority to control all substantial decisions of the trust (and no other person has veto power).

heading.v: What are federal income tax withholdings?

t.v: Your

is the amount of federal income tax withheld from your paycheck and other sources. If you’re an employee, your employer probably withholds income tax and pays it to the IRS in your name. Tax may also be withheld from certain other income — including pensions, bonuses, commissions, and gambling winnings.
If too little is withheld, you’ll generally owe tax when you file your tax return and may owe a penalty. If too much is withheld, you’ll generally be due a refund.
If you’re self-employed or don’t pay your taxes through withholding, you may need to pay estimated tax directly to the IRS as quarterly payments.

heading.v: What’s a 1099-G?

t.v: A 1099-G is used by federal, state, and local government agencies to report payments of unemployment compensation and other kinds of government payments.
Depending on the agency that issued it, 1099-G forms may look different, but they should all have the name "Certain Government Payments" on the form.
Anyone who received
or more in unemployment compensation in one tax year should get a 1099-G from their state unemployment agency reporting what was paid.
You may not get a 1099-G if the unemployment compensation was under
, but you’re still required to report it.

Most agencies provide a paper copy of a 1099-G by January 31 of each year. If you lost or never received your 1099-G, ask the agency that made the payments for a copy. If you still haven’t received the missing form(s) by the end of February, call the IRS at
for help.
If you get an unexpected 1099-G for unemployment compensation, it’s possible that someone may be using your information to fraudulently receive unemployment benefits.
If this happens, don’t include this on your federal tax return. Contact your state unemployment agency and request a corrected form showing $0 benefits received.

heading.v: What are dependent care benefits?

t.v: Dependent care benefits are provided by an employer and used to care for dependents, such as young children and family members with disabilities.
Dependent care benefits can include:
Pre-tax contributions you made under a dependent care flexible spending arrangement (FSA)
Amounts your employer paid directly to either you or your care provider for the care of a qualifying person while you work or look for work
The fair market value of care in a daycare facility provided or sponsored by your employer
When you get dependent care benefits from your employer, they’re tax-free. But, in some cases you may need to pay taxes on these benefits later when you file your taxes.

heading.v: What are qualified dependent care expenses?

t.v: Qualified expenses include amounts paid for the care of a qualifying person while you (or your spouse if you’re filing jointly) worked or looked for work. The main purpose of the care must be for the qualifying person’s well-being and protection.
Qualified expenses must be paid to a qualified care provider. According to the IRS, a qualified care provider cannot be:
Your dependent
Your spouse (at any time in
The parent of your qualifying child
Your biological child, adopted child, stepchild, or foster child unless they were age 19 or older by the end of
Some expenses that may qualify:
Household services that are at least partly for the care of a qualifying person and that are needed to run a home, like the services of a cook, maid, babysitter, housekeeper, or cleaning person
Expenses for a child in nursery school, preschool, or similar programs for children below kindergarten level
Expenses for before- or after-school care of a child in kindergarten or a higher grade
Expenses for day camp
Expenses for a dependent care center that complies with state and local regulations
Fees paid to an agency to get care provider services
Deposits and application fees paid to an agency or preschool (as long as they weren’t forfeited)
Some expenses that don’t qualify:
Expenses to attend kindergarten or a higher grade
Summer school and tutoring programs
Overnight camps
Expenses for food, lodging, clothing, education, entertainment, unless they were related to the care of the qualifying person and can’t be separated from the total cost
Child support payments
This is not a complete list. Refer to
to learn more about which expenses qualify.

heading.v: What’s a Health Savings Account (HSA)?

t.v: An HSA is a type of savings account that lets you set aside money on a pre-tax basis to pay for qualified medical expenses.
You can use the funds in an HSA at any time to pay for qualified medical expenses. But you may contribute to an HSA only if you meet certain requirements, including that you:
Have a High-Deductible Health Plan
Have no other health coverage except certain allowed coverage
Aren’t enrolled in Medicare
Can’t be claimed as someone else’s dependent in

heading.v: What’s a Form 1099-SA?

t.v: Form 1099-SA is issued by Health Savings Account (HSA) trustees, like banks or insurance companies, to report distribution amounts made that year from an HSA to pay for qualified medical expenses.
Depending on who issued it, Forms 1099-SA may look different, but they should all have the name "Distributions From an HSA, Archer MSA, or Medicare Advantage MSA" on the form.
Usually, taxpayers who have taken a distribution in
get a Form 1099-SA by January 31,
Even if you didn’t get a Form 1099-SA, you’re still required to report any distributions taken from an HSA on your federal tax return.

c.v: What if I’m missing a Form 1099-SA?

t.v: If you lost or never received your Form 1099-SA, ask your HSA trustee for a copy.

heading.v: What are qualified medical expenses for a Health Savings Account (HSA)?

t.v: Generally, qualified medical expenses for HSA purposes are medical expenses that weren’t covered by an insurance plan. They include many types of medical expenses (outlined in more detail in
), as well as some general health expenses such as:
Nonprescription medication
Menstrual care products, like tampons and pads
Personal protective equipment, such as masks and hand sanitizer, to prevent the spread of COVID-19
Home testing for COVID-19
In order to qualify, medical expenses must be taken after an HSA was established.
Refer to

c.v: Publication 969, Health Savings Accounts and Other Tax-Favored Health Plans

t.v: for more on qualified medical expenses.

heading.v: What is a Health Savings Account (HSA) rollover or a trustee-to-trustee transfer?

t.v: A

is a tax-free distribution (withdrawal) of funds from one HSA that is reinvested into another HSA of the same account beneficiary. Generally, you must complete the rollover within 60 days after you received the distribution. An HSA can only receive one rollover contribution during a 1-year period.
In a

, you instruct the trustee of your HSA to transfer funds directly to the trustee of another of your HSAs. This transfer isn’t considered a rollover. There is no limit on the number of these transfers.
Rollovers and trustee-to-trustee transfers aren’t included in your income, aren’t eligible for the HSA deduction, and don’t reduce your contribution limit.

heading.v: How are taxable Health Savings Account (HSA) distributions calculated?

t.v: Distributions used for qualified medical expenses aren’t taxable. If the amount of distributions (
minus any rollovers or withdrawn excess contributions) is equal to the amount of qualified medical expenses, then the taxable distribution amount is $0.

If the amount of distributions is greater than the amount of qualified medical expenses, then this extra amount is taxable income. An additional 20% tax is applied, unless the distributions were made after the account beneficiary:
Died
Became disabled
Turned age 65
Direct File doesn’t yet support taxable HSA distributions.

heading.v: What are qualified medical expenses for a Health Savings Account (HSA)?

t.v: Generally, qualified medical expenses for HSA purposes are medical expenses that weren’t covered by an insurance plan. They include many types of medical expenses (outlined in more detail in
), as well as some general health expenses such as:
Nonprescription medication
Menstrual care products, like tampons and pads
Personal protective equipment, such as masks and hand sanitizer, to prevent the spread of COVID-19
Home testing for COVID-19
In order to qualify, medical expenses must be taken after an HSA was established.
Refer to

heading.v: Whose medical expenses can be covered by Health Savings Account (HSA) distributions?

t.v: If you have a self-only plan, include medical expenses for yourself.
If you have a family plan, include medical expenses for yourself, your spouse, and your dependents.
If you have a family plan, you can also include medical expenses from these situations:
Any medical expenses that you paid for any person who would have been considered your dependent except that:
They filed a joint return
They had gross income
You, or your spouse if filing jointly, are dependents of someone else

Parents who are divorced, separated, or living apart for the last 6 months of the calendar year can treat their child (or children) as the dependent of both parents, whether or not the custodial parent releases claim to the child as the custodial parent’s dependent.
In this situation, either parent can cover qualified medical expenses for the child with HSA distributions.

heading.v: The Premium Tax Credit (PTC)

t.v: The PTC helps eligible people cover their premiums (monthly payments) for health insurance purchased through a government Marketplace like HealthCare.gov or a state Marketplace or exchange.
To get this credit, you must meet certain requirements and file a tax return with Form 8962, Premium Tax Credit (PTC).
Most people who qualify for the PTC get the credit in advance to help pay their monthly health insurance premiums throughout the year.
These advance payments of PTC are made by the Marketplace directly to the insurance provider on a person’s behalf.
When you file your taxes, the amount of the credit you got in advance is compared to the  amount you actually qualify for.
If you didn’t get the full amount that you qualify for through advance payments, you’ll get the remaining credit when you file your taxes.
If your advance payments are more than the PTC you qualify for, you’ll have to repay some or all of the excess amount on your federal tax return.

heading.v: What are advance payments of Premium Tax Credit (PTC)?

t.v: When you enroll in a qualified Marketplace health plan, you estimate your expected income and family size for the year of coverage. Based on this information, the Marketplace estimates the amount of monthly PTC you’ll be allowed for the year of coverage. You can then decide to use any amount of PTC  in advance to lower your monthly health insurance premiums.
Most people who qualify for the PTC choose to get it in advance to help pay their monthly health insurance premiums throughout the year.
These advance payments of PTC are made by the Marketplace directly to the insurance provider on a person’s behalf.
Advance payments are sometimes referred to as a "subsidy," "tax credit," or "APTC."

heading.v: What’s employer-sponsored health coverage?

t.v: Employer-sponsored health coverage is provided by an employer and offered to employees and their families.
Employer-sponsored coverage may include group health insurance coverage such as:
An insured plan or coverage offered in the small or large group market within a state
A governmental plan, such as the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program
A grandfathered health plan offered in a group market
Employer-sponsored coverage may also include:
A self-insured health plan
Individual coverage Health Reimbursement Arrangements (HRAs)
COBRA coverage
Retiree coverage
Coverage under an expatriate health plan
The Nonappropriated Fund Health Benefits Program of the Department of Defense

Effects of alcohol or drug abuse by the victim’s spouse
Abuse of a child or other family member living in the household

heading.v: What’s Minimum Essential Coverage (MEC)?

t.v: Certain government-sponsored health coverage is Minimum Essential Coverage (MEC). You generally can’t take the Premium Tax Credit (PTC) for a person in your tax family for any months when they were eligible for other MEC including:
Medicaid (except for certain limited scope programs)
Medicare Part A
Medicare Advantage plans
The Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP)
The Department of Veterans Affairs medical benefits package for eligible veterans
Civilian Health and Medical Program of the Department of Veterans Affairs (CHAMPVA)
Comprehensive health care for children with spina bifida who are the children of Vietnam veterans and veterans of covered service in Korea
TRICARE
Health coverage for Peace Corps volunteers
Other health coverage designated by the Department of Health and Human Services
Individual market coverage is considered MEC, but if someone was enrolled in or eligible for individual market coverage, they can still qualify for the PTC.
A person’s eligibility for Medicaid or CHIP is decided when they enroll in the qualified health plan. That

c.v: eligibility decision applies for the entire year

t.v: (even if your family size or household income changes).

heading.v: When are enrollment premiums considered paid in full?

t.v: Enrollment premiums are the amount paid each month for health insurance. Enrollment premiums are considered paid in full when:
Someone pays the premiums on behalf of the person enrolled in the coverage before the federal tax filing deadline
The premiums are paid with advance payments of the Premium Tax Credit (PTC)
For anyone who had a successful eligibility appeal, became eligible for advance payments of PTC, and retroactively enrolled in a qualified Marketplace health plan:
The enrollment premiums are considered paid in full if your advance payments of PTC cover the full amount of the enrollment premiums

If your advance payments of PTC don’t cover the full amount of the enrollment premiums, you must pay the remaining amount within 120 days after your appeal date for the premiums to be considered paid in full

heading.v: The Premium Tax Credit (PTC)

t.v: The PTC helps eligible people cover their premiums (monthly payments) for health insurance purchased through a government Marketplace like HealthCare.gov or a state Marketplace or exchange.
To get this credit, you must meet certain requirements and file a tax return with Form 8962, Premium Tax Credit (PTC).
Most people who qualify for the PTC get the credit in advance to help pay their monthly health insurance premiums throughout the year.
These advance payments of PTC are made by the Marketplace directly to the insurance provider on a person’s behalf.
When you file your taxes, the amount of the credit you got in advance is compared to the  amount you actually qualify for.
If you didn’t get the full amount that you qualify for through advance payments, you’ll get the remaining credit when you file your taxes.
If your advance payments are more than the PTC you qualify for, you’ll have to repay some or all of the excess amount on your federal tax return.

heading.v: How is a repayment limitation calculated?

t.v: When calculating how much excess advance Premium Tax Credit (PTC) you’ll need to repay, the IRS uses repayment limitations shown in Table 5 of the instructions for Form 8962.
Your repayment of excess advance PTC may be limited (lowered) if your household income is below 400% of the federal poverty line for your family size.

heading.v: How is excess advance Premium Tax Credit (PTC) calculated?

t.v: When you enroll in a qualified Marketplace health plan, you estimate your expected income and family size for the year of coverage. Based on this information, the Marketplace estimates the amount of monthly PTC you’ll be allowed for the year of coverage. You can then decide to use any amount of PTC in advance to lower your monthly health insurance premiums.
At the end of the tax year, you’ll know your actual income and family size. You use this to figure out whether you qualify for the PTC in
and the amount of credit you’re allowed to take.
If you had advance payments of PTC, we use Form 8962 to compare those advance payments with your actual PTC.
If the advance payments of PTC are more than your PTC, you have excess advance PTC and must repay some or all of the difference.
If you didn’t qualify for PTC but had advance payments of PTC, you have to repay some or all of your advance payments.
Your repayment amount may be limited (lowered) if your household income is below 400% of the federal poverty line for your family size.

t.v: When you enroll in a qualified Marketplace health plan, you estimate your expected income and family size for the year of coverage. Based on this information, the Marketplace estimates the amount of monthly PTC you’ll be allowed for the year of coverage. You can then decide to use any amount of PTC in advance to lower your monthly health insurance premiums.
At the end of the tax year, you’ll know your actual income and family size. You use this to figure out whether you qualify for the PTC in
and the amount of credit you’re allowed to take.
If you had advance payments of PTC, we use Form 8962 to compare those advance payments with your actual PTC.
If the advance payments of PTC are more than your PTC, you have excess advance PTC and must repay some or all of the difference.
If you didn’t qualify for PTC but had advance payments of PTC, you have to repay some or all of your advance payments.
Your repayment amount may be limited (lowered) if your household income is below 400% of the federal poverty line for your family size.

heading.v: How is a repayment limitation calculated?

t.v: When calculating how much excess advance Premium Tax Credit (PTC) you’ll need to repay, the IRS uses repayment limitations shown in Table 5 of the instructions for Form 8962.
Your repayment of excess advance PTC may be limited (lowered) if your household income is below 400% of the federal poverty line for your family size.

heading.v: What are qualified dependent care expenses?

t.v: Qualified expenses include amounts paid for the care of a qualifying person while you (or your spouse if you’re filing jointly) worked or looked for work. The main purpose of the care must be for the qualifying person’s well-being and protection.
Qualified expenses must be paid to a qualified care provider. According to the IRS, a qualified care provider cannot be:
Your dependent
Your spouse (at any time in
The parent of your qualifying child
Your biological child, adopted child, stepchild, or foster child unless they were age 19 or older by the end of
Some expenses that may qualify:
Household services that are at least partly for the care of a qualifying person and that are needed to run a home, like the services of a cook, maid, babysitter, housekeeper, or cleaning person
Expenses for a child in nursery school, preschool, or similar programs for children below kindergarten level
Expenses for before- or after-school care of a child in kindergarten or a higher grade
Expenses for day camp
Expenses for a dependent care center that complies with state and local regulations
Fees paid to an agency to get care provider services
Deposits and application fees paid to an agency or preschool (as long as they weren’t forfeited)
Some expenses that don’t qualify:
Expenses to attend kindergarten or a higher grade
Summer school and tutoring programs
Overnight camps
Expenses for food, lodging, clothing, education, entertainment, unless they were related to the care of the qualifying person and can’t be separated from the total cost
Child support payments
This is not a complete list. Refer to
to learn more about which expenses qualify.

heading.v: What taxable payments qualify as disability income for the Credit for the Elderly or the Disabled?

t.v: Many types of disability payments are nontaxable and don’t count as income for tax purposes. However, you do pay taxes on any disability payments you receive that meet both of these requirements:
Paid under your employer’s accident and health plan
Included in your income as wages (or payments instead of wages) for the time you’re absent from work because of permanent and total disability. This would be reported on a Form W-2
If you had this type of taxable disability income, the Credit for the Elderly or the Disabled could help offset taxes owed on this income.
Don’t include any payments from an employer plan if:
The plan doesn’t provide for disability retirement
Payments were received after you reached the mandatory retirement age
They were lump-sum payments for accrued annual leave that you received when you retired on disability
Do not include Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) payments, even if taxable.

t.v: You are the qualifying child of another taxpayer for the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) if
of these are true.
You are that person’s:
Child, stepchild, foster child, or a descendant of any of them, or
Sibling, half sibling, step sibling, or a descendant of any of them
You were:
Under age 19 at the end of the year and younger than that person (or that person’s spouse, if they filed jointly), or
Under age 24 at the end of the year, a student, and younger than that person (or that person’s spouse, if they filed jointly), or
Any age and had a permanent disability that prevented you from working and making money
In
, you lived with that person in the United States for more than 6 months.
You aren’t filing a joint return for the year, or you’re filing a joint return only to get a refund of money you paid toward taxes.
If
of these statements are true, you are the qualifying child of another taxpayer for EITC, even if they don’t claim the credit or don’t meet all of the rules to claim it.

t.v: Some credits are
. This means that they can reduce your taxes, but they won’t reduce what you owe below $0 and they won’t give you a refund
Nonrefundable credits:
Child and Dependent Care Credit
Credit for the Elderly or the Disabled
Savers Credit
Credit for Other Dependents
Child Tax Credit
For example, if you’re eligible to take a $2,000 Child and Dependent Care Credit but you only owe $1,000 in taxes, you can only reduce your taxes by $1,000, not the full $2,000.
If you already used the Child and Dependent Care Credit to reduce your tax bill to $0, you won’t be able to apply other nonrefundable credits to your taxes, even if you’re eligible for them.

heading.v: The Premium Tax Credit (PTC)

t.v: The PTC helps eligible people cover their premiums (monthly payments) for health insurance purchased through a government Marketplace like HealthCare.gov or a state Marketplace or exchange.
To get this credit, you must meet certain requirements and file a tax return with Form 8962, Premium Tax Credit (PTC).
Most people who qualify for the PTC get the credit in advance to help pay their monthly health insurance premiums throughout the year.
These advance payments of PTC are made by the Marketplace directly to the insurance provider on a person’s behalf.
When you file your taxes, the amount of the credit you got in advance is compared to the  amount you actually qualify for.
If you didn’t get the full amount that you qualify for through advance payments, you’ll get the remaining credit when you file your taxes.
If your advance payments are more than the PTC you qualify for, you’ll have to repay some or all of the excess amount on your federal tax return.

heading.v: What are federal income tax withholdings?

t.v: Your

is the amount of federal income tax withheld from your paycheck and other sources. If you’re an employee, your employer probably withholds income tax and pays it to the IRS in your name. Tax may also be withheld from certain other income — including pensions, bonuses, commissions, and gambling winnings.
If too little is withheld, you’ll generally owe tax when you file your tax return and may owe a penalty. If too much is withheld, you’ll generally be due a refund.
If you’re self-employed or don’t pay your taxes through withholding, you may need to pay estimated tax directly to the IRS as quarterly payments.

heading.v: What does it mean to owe federal taxes?

t.v: This means that your total payments were less than the federal tax you owed.
Taxpayers pay federal income tax throughout the year in the form of withholdings and estimated tax payments.
What are withholdings?

Your withholding is the amount of federal income tax withheld from your paycheck and other sources. If you’re an employee, your employer probably withholds income tax and pays it to the IRS in your name. Tax may also be withheld from certain other income — including pensions, bonuses, commissions, and gambling winnings.
If too little is withheld, you’ll generally owe tax when you file your tax return and may owe a penalty. If too much is withheld, you’ll generally be due a refund.
What are estimated tax payments?

Estimated tax payments are tax payments you made on income that can be taxed but isn’t subject to withholding. If you don’t pay your taxes through withholding, or don’t pay enough tax that way, you may need to pay estimated tax directly to the IRS as quarterly payments. People who are self-employed generally pay their tax this way.

heading.v: What does it mean to get a federal tax refund?

t.v: This means that your total payments were more than the federal tax you owed. The government owes you a refund of what you paid over what you owe.

heading.v: How is excess advance Premium Tax Credit (PTC) calculated?

t.v: When you enroll in a qualified Marketplace health plan, you estimate your expected income and family size for the year of coverage. Based on this information, the Marketplace estimates the amount of monthly PTC you’ll be allowed for the year of coverage. You can then decide to use any amount of PTC in advance to lower your monthly health insurance premiums.
At the end of the tax year, you’ll know your actual income and family size. You use this to figure out whether you qualify for the PTC in
and the amount of credit you’re allowed to take.
If you had advance payments of PTC, we use Form 8962 to compare those advance payments with your actual PTC.
If the advance payments of PTC are more than your PTC, you have excess advance PTC and must repay some or all of the difference.
If you didn’t qualify for PTC but had advance payments of PTC, you have to repay some or all of your advance payments.
Your repayment amount may be limited (lowered) if your household income is below 400% of the federal poverty line for your family size.

heading.v: What are nonrefundable credits?

t.v: Some credits are
. This means that they can reduce your taxes, but they won’t reduce what you owe below $0 and they won’t give you a refund
Nonrefundable credits:
Child and Dependent Care Credit
Credit for the Elderly or the Disabled
Child Tax Credit

For example, if you’re eligible to take a $2,000 Child Tax Credit but you only owe $1,000 in taxes, you can only reduce your taxes by $1,000, not the full $2,000.
If you already used the Child Tax Credit to reduce your tax bill to $0, you won’t be able to apply other nonrefundable credits to your taxes, even if you’re eligible for them.

<InternalLink>.because: every remaining one points at a `/data-view/…` route. This port has no DataView, since the topic page is its review surface, so there is nowhere to link to. The words survive without the link.

<InlinePDFButton>.because: out of scope: PDF. The sentence around it survives, without the download button.
